title: Tunable Selectivity for Electrochemical CO2 Reduction by Bimetallic Cu–Sn Catalysts: Elucidating the Roles of Cu and Sn
abstract: Production of formate or CO from electrochemical CO2 reduction reactions (eCO2RRs) represents a promising way to utilize CO2 with future low-carbon electricity to produce value-added chemicals and fuels. Herein, a series of Cu−Sn composite catalysts were designed for eCO2RRs. The reduction products could be tuned selectively from formate to CO by varying the Cu/Sn composition. The catalyst Cu1Sn1 with a CuSn alloy core and a SnO shell structure doped with a small amount of Cu gives a maximum faradic efficiency (FE) of 95.4 for formate at −1.2 V. In contrast, the single-Sn-atom-doped Cu of Cu20Sn1 is selective to CO with a maximum FE of 95.3% at −1.0 V. The DFT results reveal that the existence of small amounts of Cu or Sn single atoms in these two catalysts is critical to reducing the reaction free energies of CO2 reduction, resulting in the selective formation of formate and CO, respectively.

KEYWORDS: bimetallic Cu−Sn catalyst, composition, CO2 reduction, formate, CO, selectivity
■ INTRODUCTION Electrochemical CO2 reduction reactions (eCO2RRs) under ambient conditions are a promising strategy to utilize and store low-carbon electricity for converting CO2 to valuable products and e-fuels.1 For example, formate can be used as a hydrogen energy carrier for fuel cells2−4 and biomass upgrading.5,6 CO could be further electrochemically reduced to hydrocarbons.7−9 After decades of research, it has been well established that the CO2 reduction activity and selectivity are highly related to the binding strength of reaction intermediates on the catalyst surface.10−12 For instance, the selectivity for formate or CO of Sn-based catalyst is not high enough because of the scaling relationship between the *OCHO and *COOH reaction intermediates.13−16 Although nanostructure engineering was introduced to alter the binding strength of specific reaction intermediate on Sn-based catalysts by adjusting their sizes,17 oxidation state,18,19 and grain boundaries,20,21 it remains challenging to break this relationship limited by their intrinsic properties. Recently, experiments demonstrated that the activity and
selectivity of Sn-based catalysts for eCO2RR to formate or CO were significantly enhanced after modification with other metals, such as Cu,22−27 Ag,28 Pd,29 and Ti.30 Among them, Cu is more attractive because of its tunable selectivity for CO2 reduction and earth abundance.31,32 Therefore, Cu−Sn-based catalysts were extensively studied for eCO2RR. To date, only a few studies revealed that the selectivity of Cu−Sn bimetallic catalysts can be tuned from HCOOH to CO by altering the
Cu/Sn composition.22,23,27 However, insufficient selectivity remains an issue, and the origin of high faradic efficiency (FE) of HCOOH or CO for the Cu−Sn bimetallic catalysts is still under debate. It is thus essential to design new Cu−Sn composite catalysts for selective eCO2RR at a high yield and offer a platform to understand the role of Cu and Sn in the bimetallic system. In this work, we reported a series of bimetallic Cu−Sn
composite catalysts with tunable chemical composition for eCO2RR. As illustrated in Figure 1, these catalysts were prepared by reducing CuCl2·2H2O and SnCl2·2H2O in an aqueous solution with sodium borohydride as the reductive agent. Pure Cu and Sn were also prepared as the reference in the same way. The prepared catalysts were denoted as CuxSny, and the x/y represent Cu/Sn feed molar ratio in the reaction (Cu/Sn ratio: from 50/1 to 1/2). Electrocatalytic measurements reveal that the products of CO2 reduction can be tuned selectively from HCOOH to CO by systematically varying the Cu/Sn ratio. As an ideal catalyst model, a linear relationship between the selectivity of CO2 reduction and Cu/Sn composition was formed. Compared with pure Cu or Sn

particles, catalysts Cu1Sn1 (consisting of CuSn alloy core and a small amount of the Cu-doped SnO shell) and Cu20Sn1 (consisting of single-Sn-atom-doped Cu) exhibited high FEs of 86.6−95.8% for HCOOH at −0.8 to −1.2 V (vs reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE), same hereinafter) and of 92.2− 95.3% for CO at −0.7 to −1.0 V, respectively, as well as good stability for over 10 h. Over a wide potential window, the selectivity is higher than those reported for product tunable Cu−Sn-based catalysts to date with high catalytic activity.22,23,27
■ RESULTS AND DISCUSSION The morphology of the as-prepared Cu−Sn catalysts (Figure S1) and the reference samples (Figure S2) were characterized by transmission electron microscopy (TEM). As depicted, bimetallic Cu−Sn catalysts consist of small irregularly shaped particles with sizes ranging from 20 to 100 nm and pure Cu and pure Sn particles with sizes of 10−50 and 300−500 nm, respectively. Then, powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) was carried out to analyze the crystal structures of these catalysts (Figures S3 and S4). As depicted, pure Sn particles possess an Sn phase. In the catalyst of Cu1Sn2 and Cu1Sn1, both Sn and CuSn alloy phases were indexed, but the Sn phase intensity in Cu1Sn1 is very weak. The CuSn alloy is the only phase observed in Cu2Sn1. For Cu4Sn1, apart from the CuSn alloy phase, the Cu2O phase was also detected. In the catalysts with a Cu/Sn ratio of >4 and pure Cu, the diffraction peaks at ∼36.4° (2θ) and ∼42.5° could be indexed to the CuO phase, whereas the peak at ∼50.4° could be attributed to Cu. In these catalysts, no diffraction related to Sn oxide species was detected, which could be attributed to the small distribution and/or the amorphous structure. The chemical state of Cu and Sn were studied by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS)
analysis. Figure S5 shows the Cu 2p XPS and Cu LMM auger spectrum. In the catalysts with a Cu/Sn ratio ≤4, the Cu 2p peaks at ∼932.4 and ∼952.1 eV confirm the existence of Cu+ and/or Cu0 species, respectively. Further, the Cu LMM auger spectrum indicates that the Cu peaks at ∼916.0 eV (Cu1+) and ∼918.6 (Cu0) demonstrate the coexistence of Cu0 and Cu1+.33−35 For the catalysts with a Cu/Sn ratio >4, a shift of the Cu 2p peaks to ∼933.4 and ∼953.4 eV along with two strong satellite peaks are characteristic of Cu2+, and also a peak at ∼917.7 eV (Cu2+) in the Cu LMM auger spectrum indicates the formation of CuO species.36,37 Further, the Sn 3d XPS survey in Figure S6 shows that Sn0 (∼486.3 and ∼494.7 eV) exists in the catalysts with the Cu/Sn ratio ≤4,38 and all Cu− Sn catalysts are comprised of Sn2+ (∼484.2 and ∼493.0 eV).21,22
To get a close examination of the Cu−Sn catalysts, highresolution TEM (HRTEM) was employed by taking Cu1Sn1 and Cu20Sn1 as representative examples. As shown in Figure S7, the CuSn alloy surrounded by an amorphous layer was confirmed for Cu1Sn1, resulting in a core−shell structure. The lattice spacing of 0.209 nm in Figure S7a and 0.301 nm in Figure S7b correspond to the CuSn(110) and (101) planes, respectively.39 The amorphous shell thickness was determined to be 2−6 nm. In the case of Cu20Sn1 (Figure S8), the lattice spacing of 0.177 and 0.254 nm are assigned to Cu(200)27 and CuO(002)40 planes, respectively. Crystalline Cu and CuO and some amorphous structures were detected. Consequently, aberration-corrected high-angle annular dark-field scanning TEM (HAADF-STEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) elemental mapping were used to reveal the distribution of Cu and Sn in the catalysts. As displayed in Figures 2a−e and S9, most Cu elements are confined to the core, and a uniform Sn, O, and very fewer Cu elements are concentrated at the shell of Cu1Sn1. Combined with XPS and HRTEM analysis, the O and Sn species are likely associated with the amorphous structure, implying that a CuSn alloy core and a Cu-doped SnO shell structure were formed. Figures 2f−j and S10 show the EDS analysis of Cu20Sn1, and the results indicate that the Cu and Sn elements are distributed throughout the particle. Using inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES), the Cu/Sn molar ratio in Cu1Sn1 and Cu20Sn1 was measured to be 1.07 and 20.49, respectively. These results are close to the nominal molar ratio of Cu and Sn used in the synthesis. The electrocatalytic properties of the Cu−Sn catalysts were
evaluated by a three-electrode gas-tight H-cell reactor. A cathodic electrode was prepared by dropping cast catalyst dispersion on carbon paper and dried at room temperature.

Figures S11 and S12 are the cyclic voltammetry (CV) results of the prepared catalysts and blank carbon paper in Ar- and CO2saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte. For pure Sn, an increased current density (geometric current density) was observed in the CO2-saturated electrolyte when compared to the Arsaturated one, while its total current density is less than 10 mA cm−2 in the test potential range. On the pure Cu, no obvious total current density gap between Ar- and CO2-saturated electrolytes indicates that hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) is the dominant reaction. In stark contrast, all of the bimetallic Cu−Sn catalysts show an obvious enhanced current density when switching the saturated electrolyte from Ar to CO2, and their current density is much higher than that of pure Sn and pure Cu. These results revealed a high activity of bimetallic Cu−Sn catalysts toward CO2 reduction. To assess the catalytic selectivity, potential-dependent faradic efficiencies (FEs) were measured and gas and liquid products were quantified by online gas chromatography and 1H nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), respectively. To calculate the faradic efficiency of specific products, calibration curves of gas and liquid products were used (Figure S13). As displayed in Figure 3a, the major product of pure Sn is
HCOOH, consistent with the reported Sn-based catalysts.13 However, the FE for HCOOH is less than 80% over the whole studied potential range. In the case of pure Cu (Figure 3b), the total FE of CO2 reduction is less than 50% and CO and HCOOH are the major products with small amounts of CH4, ethylene, ethanol, n-propanol, and acetate. In contrast, based on FE for CO2 reduction products (Figures 3c,d and S14), the Cu−Sn catalysts show prominent suppression of hydrogen evolution, suggesting an enhanced electrocatalytic CO2 reduction selectivity due to the synergy of Cu and Sn. For
example, catalysts with a Cu/Sn ratio ≤2 show a high CO2 reduction selectivity to formate (Figures 3c and S14a,b). In particular, Cu1Sn1 gives the best activity and selectivity with FE ≥86.6% for formate at −0.8 to −1.1 V (Figure 3c). At more negative potential, such as −1.2 and −1.3 V, the FE for formate could reach 95.8 and 94.8%, respectively. Consequently, the formate partial current density at these two potentials was determined to be 24.1 and 30.3 mA cm−2, respectively. Accordingly, the formation amount of HCOOH in the catalyst Cu1Sn1 in each test is shown in Figure S15. To gain more insights into the effect of the Cu/Sn ratio on the FEs for CO2 reduction products, the product distribution of higher Cu amount catalysts, such as Cu4Sn1, Cu6Sn1, and Cu8Sn1, was also analyzed. As shown in Figure S14c−e, increasing the Cu/ Sn ratio resulted in a significant decrease in formate selectivity to favor CO formation. Notably, the FE of Cu8Sn1 for CO exceeded that for HCOOH at −0.8 and −0.9 V (Figure S14e). At high Cu concentrations, catalyst Cu20Sn1 reached the FE of 79.7% at −0.6 V and quickly to 93.3% at −0.7 V (Figure 3d). At −0.6 and −0.7 V, only a trace amount of H2 was produced with no HCOOH. Moreover, the FE for CO was maintained above 92.2% and HCOOH increased a little to 4.6% at the applied potentials from −0.8 to −1.0 V. The maximum FE of Cu20Sn1 for CO is 95.3%, which is achieved at −1.0 V with a partial current density of 12.5 mA cm−2. Similarly, catalyst Cu50Sn1 also shows a distinct preference for CO formation but lower FE and current density than those of Cu20Sn1 (Figure S14f). Overall, Cu1Sn1 and Cu20Sn1 were confirmed to have the highest selectivity toward formate and CO, respectively, comparable or even superior to those of reported Cu−Snbased catalysts (Table S1). Moreover, when a 10 h continuous operation was performed at −0.9 V on Cu1Sn1 and Cu20Sn1 (Figure 3e,f), both catalysts maintained a stable current density and FE with a slight loss of performance, suggesting that these two catalysts are stable. To better reflect the real catalytic activity toward CO2 reduction, potential-dependent total current density and formate (CO) partial current density of Cu1Sn1 (Cu20Sn1) were plotted and compared with pure Sn and Cu (Figure S16). The results prove that the coupling of Sn with Cu with a proper Cu/Sn ratio leads to high CO2 reduction activity and selectivity. To figure out why both Cu1Sn1 and Cu20Sn1 show a higher current density than those of pure Sn and Cu, electrochemical surface area (ECSA) of these four catalysts were determined by measuring the doublelayer capacitance (Cdl) (Figure S17 and Table S2), followed by the current density normalization based on the obtained ECSA. The normalized current density (jECSA) of Cu1Sn1, Cu20Sn1, Sn, and Cu is shown in Figure S18. The results show that catalysts Cu20Sn1 and Cu1Sn1 with higher catalytic activity have less ECSA than those of Sn and Cu. Thus, the higher current densities of catalysts Cu1Sn1 and Cu20Sn1 mainly come from their intrinsic nature and not from the change in surface area. Then, the FEs for formate and CO of Cu−Sn catalysts (at −0.8 V) were plotted as a function of the Cu/Sn ratio (Figure S19), demonstrating the selective formation of formate or CO is strongly dependent on the Cu/Sn ratio. To investigate the local bonding environment and oxidation
information of the as-prepared Cu1Sn1 and Cu20Sn1 catalysts, X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) and Fourier transform extended X-ray absorption fine structure (FTEXAFS) were further applied. Figure 4a is the Cu K-edge XANES spectrum of the pristine Cu1Sn1, Cu20Sn1, and reference samples. As depicted, the pristine Cu1Sn1 catalyst

shows a similar XANES spectrum in comparison with Cu2O reference samples, verifying that the Cu1Sn1 catalyst mainly contains Cu+ species. For the pristine Cu20Sn1 catalyst, the XANES spectrum is situated between the Cu2O and CuO reference samples, indicating that Cu species in Cu20Sn1 has a valence between 1 and 2, coincident with the XPS analysis. Meanwhile, we also analyzed their FT-EXAFS spectrum of the Cu K-edge in R-space. As displayed in Figure 4b, both pristine Cu1Sn1 and Cu20Sn1 catalysts show a dominant Cu−O bond peak at around 1.48 Å. The difference is that pristine Cu1Sn1 has one more scattering peak between 2.08 and 2.35 Å, which could be assigned to the CuSn alloy. At the Sn K-edge, the XANES spectrum of pristine Cu1Sn1 and Cu20Sn1 catalysts were also collected and are shown in Figure 4c. The results suggest that the Sn element in pristine Cu1Sn1 has a similar absorption edge energy to that of the SnO reference sample, indicating that Sn2+ species was formed in Cu1Sn1. For catalyst Cu20Sn1, the absorption edge energy is located between SnO and SnO2 reference samples, showing that Sn species in Cu20Sn1 has a valence between 2 and 4. Accordingly, the FTEXAFS spectrum of the Sn K-edge in R-space is displayed in Figure 4d. As revealed, Cu1Sn1 shows an Sn−O bond peak at 1.56 Å, and the scattering peak between 2.05 and 2.37 Å is attributed to the SnCu alloy. In the case of Cu20Sn1, a first shell Sn−O bond peak at 1.56 Å was observed, no Sn−Sn and higher shell Sn−O bond existed, indicating that Sn atoms were atomically dispersed in the Cu substrate. To study the change in the oxidation state of Cu under reaction conditions, in situ XAS experiments at the Cu K-edge of catalysts Cu1Sn1 and Cu20Sn1 were carried out. When the potential of −1.0 V was applied during the cathodic polarization, the absorption edge energies of Cu1Sn1 and Cu20Sn1 quickly approached that of the Cu foil reference sample as the time went on (from open voltage to 20 min and then 60 min), and their EXAFS spectrum in R-space showed a peak at 2.24−2.27 Å, referring to the Cu−Sn and/or Cu−Cu bond (indistinguishable) (Figure S20).41,42 These results
demonstrate that Cu species in both of these two catalysts is in the metallic state under the reaction condition. Furthermore, the EXAFS fitting of catalysts Cu1Sn1 and Cu20Sn1 before and during the electrochemical reduction process were performed to extract the structural parameters (Figures S21−S23 and Tables S3−S5). The fitting analysis shows that the obtained scattering path and their corresponding mean bond length are consistent with the FT-EXAFS results. Moreover, the reacted Cu1Sn1 and Cu20Sn1 were characterized by HRTEM and HAADF-STEM (Figures S24 and S25), indicating that they possess the same morphology and element distribution as the freshly prepared ones. Therefore, the unique element distribution in these two catalysts may play an essential role in stabilizing *OCHO and *COOH and ultimately induce high CO2 catalytic activity and selectivity for formate and CO, respectively.26,28 To examine this hypothesis, we calculated the reaction free energies of CO2 reduction on the Sn-doped Cu(111) planes for Cu20Sn1 and the Cu-doped SnO(001) planes for Cu1Sn1, respectively (See SI for the computational details of generating these models, Figures S26 and S27). For catalyst Cu20Sn1, the ideal gas model was used to compute the zero-point energy and the entropy contribution for gas-phase CO2 and CO. As shown in Figure 5a, at 0 V vs
RHE (solid line), with the doping of Sn on the Cu surface, the reaction energy for the first electron transfer to generate *COOH decreases from 1.38 to 1.03 eV, while the free energy required for the second electron transfer to generate CO also decreases from 1.27 to 0.56 eV. Both of these decreases indicate that the doping of Sn can enhance the stabilization of reaction intermediates, well in correlation with the selective formation of CO. At −1.0 V vs RHE (dashed line in Figure 5a), Cu20Sn1 only requires 0.03 eV for the formation of *COOH, while Cu foil needs 0.38 eV, indicating the energy
https://doi.org/10.1021/acscatal.1c02556 ACS Catal. 2021, 11, 11103−11108
11106
required for the CO2 reduction is significantly decreased. In addition, the reaction free energies of CO2 reduction were also calculated on SnO, with and without the Cu substitutions (Figure 5b). With Cu doping of SnO(001) on Cu1Sn1, the reaction free energy for the formation of *OCHO decreases tremendously from 3.44 to −0.23 eV.43 These results imply that the doping effect of Cu favors the formation of *OCHO and thus the formate. In general, our DFT investigations are consistent with the hypothesis that Cu1Sn1 and Cu20Sn1 materials stabilize the formation of intermediates and enhance the selectivity of CO2 reduction.
■ CONCLUSIONS In summary, a series of Cu−Sn-based composites were developed as the model catalysts for elucidating the roles of Cu and Sn in selective eCO2RR. The eCO2RR products could be tuned selectively from formate to CO by varying the Cu/Sn composition. Compared to the reported Cu−Sn-based catalysts, the Cu1Sn1 and Cu20Sn1 are among the best catalysts with high selectivity and high partial current density of formate and CO, respectively. Characterizations reveal that catalyst Cu1Sn1 consists of a CuSn alloy core and a small amount of a Cu-doped SnO shell, while Cu20Sn1 has a single-Sn-atomdoped Cu structure. DFT calculations demonstrate that the small amount of Cu or single Sn atom in these two catalysts play an essential role in reducing the CO2 reduction free energy, thereby leading to high catalytic activity and selectivity for formate and CO, respectively. Therefore, atomically doping is the main reason why Sn couple with Cu can give rise to a distinct enhancement of the catalytic activity of Cu−Sn-based catalyst, which is different from the previously reported mechanism. These findings provide new insights into the intrinsic activity and selectivity of Cu−Sn composite catalysts for eCO2RR to formate or CO.
